# Kickoff: Solar System Quiz Pack (MTG-1)

chair: editor · invited: editor, writer-1, writer-2 · absent: none · room: story-room

## 1. Rounds: five topics with no overlap, and which facts each round owns
Round 1:
- writer-2: Split by object, so every answer has one owner. R1 The Sun (a star; light takes about 8 minutes to reach us; mostly hydrogen and helium; holds almost all the mass). R2 Rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (Mercury closest; Venus hottest; Mars red from rust/iron oxide; Olympus Mons). R3 Giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (Jupiter biggest; Great Red Spot; Saturn rings; Uranus spins on its side; Neptune farthest planet). R4 Moons: our Moon, Ganymede (largest moon), Titan (thick air), Europa (ice over an ocean). R5 Small worlds: Pluto (dwarf planet since 2006), asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, comets (ice and dust, tails point away from the Sun), meteors/shooting stars. Ownership rules: (a) a planet or moon name may be an Answer only in its owning round; (b) superlatives (biggest, hottest, closest, farthest, largest moon) belong only to the round that owns that object; (c) other rounds should not name another round answer in a Q or Why line, because the give-away check flags a line that names another round answer plus a distinctive word of its question (e.g. R4 "Ganymede orbits Jupiter, the biggest planet" would trip it; say "orbits Jupiter" only if R3 does not ask "biggest"). Safer: R4 Why lines avoid host-planet superlatives. (d) Numbers carry units and are used once in the pack (8 planets vs about 8 minutes must not both be answers). (e) No volatile facts: no moon counts (Saturn count keeps changing), no "Pluto is the ninth planet". Code-checkable ask: test that ROUNDn first line equals "# Round n: <topic>" from STYLE, and that there is no **Q5.**; today the ROUND check only requires Q1 and Q4, so a 5-question round or wrong topic would pass.
- writer-1: Five topics, split by kind of object so answers cannot collide: R1 The Sun (star, its light and heat, 8 minutes for light to reach us, center of the solar system). R2 Rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars only; e.g. Mercury closest, Venus hottest, Mars red from rust). R3 Giant planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune only; Jupiter largest, Saturn rings, Uranus tilted on its side, Neptune farthest planet). R4 Moons (Earth Moon, its phases, Titan, Europa, Io; a planet name may appear only as context, never as an answer). R5 Small bodies and exploring space (dwarf planets incl. Pluto, asteroid belt, comets, astronauts/rovers/probes). Ownership rule: every answer word belongs to exactly one round; a planet or body name is an Answer only in the round that owns it (e.g. "Mars" only in R2, "Moon" only in R4, "Pluto" only in R5). Superlatives ("largest planet", "hottest planet", "farthest") live only in the owner round, and no question in another round may mention an owned answer next to its distinctive clue (the check flags answer + distinctive question word in one line as a give-away). The style sheet should list each round owned answers so writers can check before writing, and the code rule (no Answer repeats another ROUND task) backs it. Avoid trap facts: Venus, not Mercury, is hottest; Pluto is a dwarf planet; Saturn is not the only ringed planet, so ask "best-known rings", not "only rings".
- editor: Five non-overlapping topics, each owning its facts: R1 The Sun (star, light, heat, size); R2 Rocky inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars); R3 Gas and ice giants (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune); R4 Moons (Earth's Moon and other planets' moons); R5 Small bodies and space exploration (dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, spacecraft, astronauts). A planet's moons belong to R4 only; Pluto to R5 only. No answer may repeat across rounds and no question may name another round's answer.
**Decision:** Five rounds split by kind of object; every answer has exactly one owner round. Title lines exactly: "# Round 1: The Sun" (owns: the Sun is a star, about 8 minutes for its light to reach us, mostly hydrogen and helium, holds almost all the mass, center of the solar system). "# Round 2: Rocky Planets" (owns Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars: Mercury closest to the Sun, Venus hottest because thick clouds trap heat, Mars red from rust, Olympus Mons). "# Round 3: Giant Planets" (owns Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune: Jupiter biggest, Great Red Spot, Saturn best-known rings (never "only rings"), Uranus spins on its side, Neptune farthest planet). "# Round 4: Moons" (owns our Moon and its phases, Ganymede largest moon, Titan thick air, Europa ice over an ocean, Io volcanoes). "# Round 5: Small Worlds and Space Travel" (owns Pluto as a dwarf planet since 2006, the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, comets of ice and dust with tails pointing away from the Sun, shooting stars, astronauts, rovers and probes). STYLE has the five lines "- Round n: <topic>" with exactly these topics, each followed by its owned facts. Ownership rules: a planet, moon or body name is an Answer only in its owner round; superlatives (biggest, hottest, closest, farthest, largest moon) live only in the owner round; no Q or Why line names another round answer (the give-away check flags answer plus a distinctive word of its question); no volatile facts (no moon counts, no "ninth planet"); a number is an answer at most once in the pack. Both writers proposed this split; I adopt it. writer-2 code ask (title equals the STYLE topic, no Q5) is now a rule.
- rule for STYLE*: {"mustInclude":["- Round 1: The Sun","- Round 2: Rocky Planets","- Round 3: Giant Planets","- Round 4: Moons","- Round 5: Small Worlds and Space Travel"]} (checked by code; tightened O-1)
- rule for ROUND1*: {"mustInclude":["# Round 1: The Sun"]} (checked by code; tightened O-2)
- rule for ROUND2*: {"mustInclude":["# Round 2: Rocky Planets"]} (checked by code; tightened O-3)
- rule for ROUND3*: {"mustInclude":["# Round 3: Giant Planets"]} (checked by code; tightened O-4)
- rule for ROUND4*: {"mustInclude":["# Round 4: Moons"]} (checked by code; tightened O-5)
- rule for ROUND5*: {"mustInclude":["# Round 5: Small Worlds and Space Travel"]} (checked by code; tightened O-6)
- rule for ROUND*: {"distinctAnswers":{"prefix":"**Answer:**","across":"ROUND"},"banned":["Q5"]} (checked by code; tightened O-2, O-3, O-4, O-5, O-6)
- rule for PACK*: {"mustInclude":["# Solar System Quiz Pack","# Round 1: The Sun","# Round 2: Rocky Planets","# Round 3: Giant Planets","# Round 4: Moons","# Round 5: Small Worlds and Space Travel"],"banned":["Q5"]} (checked by code; tightened O-7)

## 2. Difficulty, format and the voice of the 'why' line for ages 8-10
Round 1:
- writer-2: Format: open answers, no multiple choice. Choice lists would name other rounds answers and trip the cross-round give-away check, and they add words. Each question is three lines: "**Qn.** question?" then "**Answer:** short canonical name (1-4 words, e.g. Venus, not "It is Venus")" then "**Why:** one sentence". Canonical short answers make the repeat check meaningful. Difficulty for 8-10: per round Q1-Q2 easy (things a child may have heard: the Sun is a star, Mars is red), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a vivid reason (Venus is hotter than Mercury because thick clouds trap heat). Reading ease >= 60: questions <= 14 words, Why <= 20 words, one clause where possible, everyday words; proper nouns like Ganymede are fine but explain nothing with jargon (say "air" not "atmosphere" where it fits). Target about 140-200 words per round, inside the 100-300 limit. Voice of Why: warm and concrete, a picture or comparison a child can hold ("Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside"), never talking down, no "obviously" or "easy". Avoid banned words in natural space phrasing: no "dead star", "dead planet", "kill", or "blood-red" (say "rusty red"). Every Why must be true on its own, not just plausible; writers cite a source (NASA Solar System pages) in builder notes for each Answer.
- writer-1: Format exactly as the orders say: "# Round n: <topic>", then 4 blocks of **Qn.** question / **Answer:** short answer (one to three words, a name or number) / **Why:** one sentence. 100-300 words per round, Flesch reading ease 60+, which means short sentences and everyday words: aim for 10-14 words per sentence, explain any space word in plain terms ("a dwarf planet is a small round world"). Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy (most 8-year-olds might guess), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a fun surprise; mostly direct questions, at most one multiple choice (A/B/C) per round to vary pace. Numbers rounded and kid-sized ("about 8 minutes", "more than 1,000 Earths"), never long decimals; note "about" so the fact stays true. Voice of the Why line: warm, curious, second person where it helps ("If you could stand on Venus, you would..."), one surprising fact that teaches, never scolds a wrong guess, no scary framing; banned words stupid, dumb, kill, dead, blood, hate, and I suggest also avoiding "die"/"burn up" style phrasing. The Why must not name another round owned answer. Each round self-checks with "node meta.mjs check --order=<O>" before handing in.
- editor: Each round: title line '# Round n: <topic>', exactly 4 questions as '**Qn.** ...', '**Answer:** ...' (short, 1-5 words), '**Why:** ...' one sentence of at most 20 words, friendly and encouraging, everyday words, reading ease at least 60. Numbers as digits. No other kinds of line. Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy, Q3-Q4 a little harder. No scary or rude words.
**Decision:** Format for every round: line 1 is the title from item 1; then exactly 4 blocks, each three lines: "**Qn.** question?" (n = 1-4, at most 16 words), "**Answer:** short canonical name or number" (at most 4 words, e.g. "Venus", not "It is Venus"), "**Why:** one sentence" (at most 20 words). No other kinds of line: no intro, no notes, no multiple choice lists (open answers only; writer-1 suggested one A/B/C question per round for pace, but choice lists name other rounds answers and trip the give-away check, so pace comes from varied question forms instead). Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy (things an 8-year-old may have heard), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a fun surprise. Reading ease at least 60: short sentences, everyday words, explain any space word plainly ("air" rather than "atmosphere"). Numbers as digits (8, not eight; 1,000 not a thousand), rounded and kid-sized with "about" where needed to stay true; "one" is allowed only in phrases like "one of". Voice of the Why line: warm, curious and concrete, one surprising true fact or picture a child can hold, never talking down (no "obviously", "easy"), no scary framing (no "dead star", "blood-red"; say "rusty red"). Every Why is true on its own; writers note a source (NASA Solar System pages) for each answer in their builder notes, and self-check with node meta.mjs check --order=<O> before handing in. PACK keeps this same format plus "## Changes" with "- " lines.

- rule for PACK*: {"allowedLines":["# ","## Changes","- ","**Q","**Answer:**","**Why:**"],"lineMaxWords":[{"prefix":"**Why:**","maxWords":20},{"prefix":"**Answer:**","maxWords":4},{"prefix":"**Q","maxWords":17}],"banned":["two","three","four","five","six","seven","eight","nine","ten","eleven","twelve","twenty","thirty","forty","fifty","hundred","thousand","million","billion","obviously","atmosphere"]} (checked by code; tightened O-7)

Difficulty for 8-10: per round Q1-Q2 easy (things a child may have heard: the Sun is a star, Mars is red), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a vivid reason (Venus is hotter than Mercury because thick clouds trap heat). Reading ease >= 60: questions <= 14 words, Why <= 20 words, one clause where possible, everyday words; proper nouns like Ganymede are fine but explain nothing with jargon (say "air" not "atmosphere" where it fits). Target about 140-200 words per round, inside the 100-300 limit. Voice of Why: warm and concrete, a picture or comparison a child can hold ("Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside"), never talking down, no "obviously" or "easy". Avoid banned words in natural space phrasing: no "dead star", "dead planet", "kill", or "blood-red" (say "rusty red"). Every Why must be true on its own, not just plausible; writers cite a source (NASA Solar System pages) in builder notes for each Answer.
- writer-1: Format exactly as the orders say: "# Round n: <topic>", then 4 blocks of **Qn.** question / **Answer:** short answer (one to three words, a name or number) / **Why:** one sentence. 100-300 words per round, Flesch reading ease 60+, which means short sentences and everyday words: aim for 10-14 words per sentence, explain any space word in plain terms ("a dwarf planet is a small round world"). Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy (most 8-year-olds might guess), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a fun surprise; mostly direct questions, at most one multiple choice (A/B/C) per round to vary pace. Numbers rounded and kid-sized ("about 8 minutes", "more than 1,000 Earths"), never long decimals; note "about" so the fact stays true. Voice of the Why line: warm, curious, second person where it helps ("If you could stand on Venus, you would..."), one surprising fact that teaches, never scolds a wrong guess, no scary framing; banned words stupid, dumb, kill, dead, blood, hate, and I suggest also avoiding "die"/"burn up" style phrasing. The Why must not name another round owned answer. Each round self-checks with "node meta.mjs check --order=<O>" before handing in.

Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy, Q3-Q4 a little harder. No scary or rude words.
**Decision:** Format for every round: line 1 is the title from item 1; then exactly 4 blocks, each three lines: "**Qn.** question?" (n = 1-4, at most 16 words), "**Answer:** short canonical name or number" (at most 4 words, e.g. "Venus", not "It is Venus"), "**Why:** one sentence" (at most 20 words). No other kinds of line: no intro, no notes, no multiple choice lists (open answers only; writer-1 suggested one A/B/C question per round for pace, but choice lists name other rounds answers and trip the give-away check, so pace comes from varied question forms instead). Difficulty: Q1-Q2 easy (things an 8-year-old may have heard), Q3 medium, Q4 a stretch with a fun surprise. Reading ease at least 60: short sentences, everyday words, explain any space word plainly ("air" rather than "atmosphere"). history.findings: Class A, untrue fact (every fact must be true): (1) Q4 Why "its lakes are filled with liquid gas" -> "liquid gas" is a contradiction and misleading; Titan lakes are liquid methane and ethane, which are gases on Earth; required: a true plain wording, e.g. "its lakes hold liquid methane, a gas on Earth, instead of water". (2) Q1 "changes shape each month" -> the Moon itself does not change shape, only how much of its lit side we see; required: "seems to change shape" or "looks different" each month. (3) Q2 "the changing shapes of the Moon" -> same false implication; required: "the shapes the Moon seems to have" or similar (the Q2 Why already gives the true reason). Class B, plain words for ages 8-10 (MTG-1 item 2: explain any space word plainly): (1) Q3 Why "magnetic field" -> unexplained science term; required: drop it or explain plainly. No other defects: title, 4 blocks, word limits, banned words and ownership (Moon, phases, Ganymede, Titan are R4-owned; no other round answer named) all pass; only STYLE is shipped so no cross-round answer clash yet.

__map.learned: STYLE topics must match MTG-1 title lines exactly; list owned facts under each round line
In the Sun round, "The Sun" cannot be an answer because every question names it; use owned facts (star, mass, 8 minutes, hydrogen) as answers
Keep other rounds owned words (star, Moon, Sun-round answers) and superlatives out of Why lines; avoid naming a same-round answer in another question
Say "best known for its rings" never "only rings"; refer to the owned planet as "it" in Why lines to avoid cross-round give-aways
Rounded numbers need "about" in every line that states them, Why lines included, not just the Answer
STYLE is the first item, so there is no shipped work to cross-check; compare it line by line to the MTG-1 decision text instead.
Code check passes rounded numbers; read each Why for a flat number that needs "about" to stay true.
Code check passes literal wording; read each Q and Why for statements that are only true as appearances (Moon shape) or self-contradictory terms (liquid gas).
When only STYLE is shipped, the cross-round check is against STYLE owned facts; verify each flat number in Why lines (88 days, melt lead, Arizona width) against NASA figures.
Naming a non-answer object owned by another round (Earth, the Sun) as a comparison is allowed; only another round Answer plus its question clue is a give-away.
Read comet/meteor Why lines for what the material actually is at that moment (ice vs gas) and for always-true claims that only hold near the Sun.
On a re-check, confirm the named fix first, then re-read every line, since a revision can introduce new flat numbers or claims.

On a re-check, also verify any replacement claim a fix introduces (Ganymede wider than a small planet = wider than Mercury) and check in-round order: naming an earlier answer after it is revealed is not a give-away.
On a comet/meteor re-check, confirm both the material (gas vs ice) and the near-the-Sun qualifier, then re-verify every other line; check passed 149 words, ease 86.
For PACK, diff the body against the concatenated shipped rounds first; if identical, the job is the cross-round read (answers, superlative owners, give-aways, contradictions) plus the Changes line.
Moon Why lines can stay give-away-safe by never naming host planets; say "wider than a small planet" instead of naming Mercury.
Small-worlds lines stay give-away-safe by naming no planets: say "between the rocky and giant planets" for the asteroid belt, and keep "star" away from Sun-round question words.
Moon lines must say the Moon "seems to" change shape; name what Titan lakes hold (liquid methane) and drop unexplained terms like magnetic field.
Comet tails: say gas and dust (ice turns to gas first), and qualify that a tail only grows near the Sun.

Rounds built under strict ownership rules assemble cleanly; check cross-round lines for answer words hidden inside phrases (star in shooting stars, Sun in Away from the Sun) before calling a pack clash-free.
